preview: Yash Ogale shares his interview experience for Goldman Sachs Summer Analysts 2026, detailing the online assessment and three rounds of interviews.
content: Goldman Sachs Summer Analysts 2026 Yash Ogale Electronics and Telecommunication 2027 ynogale@gmail.com We received an email from the TPO on June 27 regarding Goldman Sachs visiting our campus. On June 30, we were informed that there would be a Goldman Sachs presentation and an Online Assessment scheduled for July 1. The presentation was from 5:00 PM to 6:00 PM, followed by the Online Assessment from 7:00 PM to 8:00 PM. During the presentation, they discussed Goldman Sachs’ principles, values, goals, and what the company does. Do not neglect this information, you never know when something from the presentation might be asked in the interviews. At the very least, make sure to note down key points or take screenshots. Online Assessment: The OA had 3 parts: - DSA - MCQs - HR question We had 3 DSA problems, I might not recollect the exact questions, since it's quite a time, but they were as follows: a) Programming Questions: i) Given a range (l, r) [l & r not included] , find pairs (x,y) in this range such that: sum of perfect divisors of x = y + 1 sum of perfect divisors of y = x + 1 x != y[Perfect divisors of a number include all divisors except the number itself.] For example, if x = 140 and y = 195, the sum of perfect divisors of x is 196 = 195+1 and that of y is 141 = 140 + 1. Constraints: r <= 50,000. ii) A problem that involved finding aliases for a particular name For example if original names = ["ABC", "DEF", "GHI"] and alias = ["AXY", "DJK", GPS"] then ABC -> AXY , DEF -> DJK , GHI -> GPS. Basically, the aliases should be mapped such that the first characters of original and alias names should be the same. iii) You were given station data for 3 weather stations for N days. Station 1 had all the data of N days perfectly, while station 2 and 3 had some missing and repeated days. The task was to find the minimum number of columns to delete such that the data is consistent. Consistency in this case meant that all 3 stations should have the same set of days (even with same counts). The test case below will make this question clear. Station 1: 1 5 7 6 4 3 2 Station 2: 5 3 3 2 2 1 4 Station 3: 3 5 4 4 4 1 6 In this case, a possible case would be to delete columns 3,4,5,7, resulting in 1 5 3 5 3 1 3 5 1 So the columns to delete are 4. We had to find the minimum possible number of columns to delete This was followed by 10 MCQs, which were a mix of CS fundamentals, aptitude, mathematics, and logical reasoning. There was also one HR question: If a teammate is facing urgent issues and cannot continue working on the project, how would you handle the situation? We got results on July 11 at around 15:00 IST, a total of 19 candidates were shortlisted for offline interviews. We got to know the interview dates on July 16 via mail. The interview was scheduled on July 19 7:00 IST Interviews: We all assembled at VJTI racing lab, since the TPO room was under renovation, sharp at 7:00 IST. You cannot afford to be late at an interview, since they might skip you if you ain’t present. There were 4 people from Goldman Sachs, and 2 people from the HR team. They addressed us shortly and said the interview will commence at 8:30. They started to call candidates in the order mentioned in the mail. I was 10th in the list. Round1 My first interview happened around 9:30, it was an HR+Tech interview.It was quite shocking since generally the first round of interview is a TECH interview. Few people had their first interview as a tech interview, but in my case the first was HR+TECH. This was somewhat close to an LLD/HLD designing round. I was called, I knocked and entered the room, he warmly greeted me. He was a chill, friendly guy, and he held some kind of aura. He asked me to introduce myself and say something which is not present in the resume. It is important to have a proper introduction beforehand, a well-structured one. Do include hobbies or some extra-curricular activities, you never know when the interviewer might ask something more about it. I shared my passion for football, leading him to ask about my playing positions and favorite club :) He then went on to ask what and how I would implement tech in the football world. I don’t remember the exact answers, but it was more of a conversation. I said I would implement computer vision to track the postures, ML for diet and even gave some past examples used in real-life football. He then went on to ask more in-depth questions about player tracking and stuff. The interview went over 60 min, and he seemed satisfied with my answers. Then he asked whether I had some questions to ask him. Here comes the important part : do ask questions, don’t just say “NO”. Do refer to the news about the company beforehand. I asked 2-3 questions, to which he replied explaining to me his answers. I said thank you for having me, and I left the room. Round 2 Around 13:00, I was called for my second interview, which was a technical round. The interviewer introduced himself, and I then introduced myself. He then gave me a paper and asked if I was comfortable with data structures, to which I confidently replied with a “YES.” You may find the question here. He clarified the question, but I still didn’t understand it completely, so I asked him further questions. It’s crucial to clarify your doubts before attempting to solve the problem. I gave him a brute-force approach with a complexity of O(N). He then asked if I could reduce the complexity further. I said, “Yeah, something close to O(log N)?” and he said yes. It took me some time to figure out a better approach. I said something co-relating the level to the number of nodes present on that level. The Nth level has 2^(N-1) nodes. This way, we could traverse leftwards up to (n-1) levels and find the number of nodes present in the first (n-1) levels. The next thing was how to calculate the number of nodes in the last layer without traversing it. I tried different things, but couldn’t figure out a proper approach. That’s when he gave me a hint, he drew a sorted array and asked me to find the floor of a number. I said, “binary search.” He said to use the same logic. I don’t remember the exact math I used, but in the end, I got the complexity down to xlog N. He then asked me to find what x would be, and I figured it would be the height of the tree so log N. So, the final complexity would be (log N)^2. Prioritize continuous communication during the interview, even when paused or problem-solving. Articulate your thought process aloud, as the interviewer is primarily interested in understanding your approach rather than just the final, optimized solution. He was satisfied with my logic. This interview went on for around 45 minutes. They shortlisted 9 candidates and asked us to assemble again after 30 minutes. I went to have my lunch. Round3 It was just over 30 minutes. I was chilling, and suddenly the HR called my name. I wasn’t mentally prepared. I somehow grabbed a pen and went inside. She guided me to one of the cabins. This was an HR round. She then asked me to brief her about my project. It’s important to have a brief description ready about your project, preferably using the STAR approach. She then went on to ask me about the rise of AI/ML and whether I was familiar with using LLMs. She also asked about group projects, any conflicts, and similar questions. It was over in 15–20 minutes, when she said, “That’s it, you can leave.” I was a bit puzzled that the interview was this short and felt a little disappointed. But later, I came to know that everyone had interviews of roughly the same duration. Lastly, it was around 17:00 when they asked us whether they were allowed to announce the results themselves. Once we agreed, they started announcing the names. I didn’t hear my name at first, and the selected candidates went inside. I felt I didn’t make the cut and stood there with a dejected look. Then one of the guys came out calling my name. I was on cloud eleven. I thanked God. They congratulated us. I came outside and called my parents to share the news. Then I called my homies, they were more happy than me :) General Preparation Tips: There is no single, universally applicable method or predefined roadmap. Practice DSA regularly For DSA i referred striver’s A2Z sheet Be consistent with your DSA preparation, avoid giving up too quickly and jumping to the solution. Struggling with a problem is natural, and I experienced this myself. After solving a problem, make sure to review the most optimized solutions to understand better approaches and improve your overall problem-solving efficiency. Learn a Language The most crucial step is to develop strong proficiency in at least one foundational programming language. In my case, this was C/C++. By “strong proficiency,” I refer to a deep understanding of the language’s core concepts, underlying mechanisms, and nuances. While much of this foundational knowledge was acquired through online resources, particularly references such as cppreference.com , the more advanced and practical understanding was developed through consistent hands-on practice. CS Fundamentals Make sure your CS Fundamentals are super strong . This includes OS, OOPS, DBMS, GFG is no doubt one of the best platforms to learn from. You can also refer to COC’s archives for relevant material. Communication To enhance your English speaking and communication abilities, active involvement in a club or community, especially in organizing events collaboratively, is highly beneficial. Alternatively, you can find resources and tips online, such as on YouTube. A key measure of effective communication is your ability to clearly explain a complex idea to someone unfamiliar with it, ensuring they achieve the same level of understanding as you do. RESUME Build a good resume : template Be thorough with every word you write in your resume. Prepare STAR-based descriptions for each project. Get your resume reviewed by seniors as early as possible and incorporate their feedback. I was fortunate to receive this feedback from Project X seniors well before the internship season began. Give Mocks The CoC regularly hosts mock interviews for its active members, where seniors offer crucial guidance on interview etiquette and expectations. Treat these sessions with seriousness, as the feedback is invaluable for performance improvement. If seniors are unavailable, actively practice with peers for continued preparation. Conclusion Compared to what I had heard from seniors from earlier batches, my interview experience felt relatively less intense. That said, interview outcomes are usually a balance of preparation and external factors , roughly 60% skill and 40% luck. Your first interview can feel overwhelming, especially when you’re surrounded by candidates who seem far more accomplished. I felt the same way. However, it’s important not to let that fear reflect in your demeanor. Present yourself as calm, composed, and confident. Answer questions with clarity and don’t let pressure affect your responses. Keep in mind that most candidates feel the same anxiety, even if they don’t show it. The interviewers are not there to trap you: they genuinely want you to do well and are supportive throughout the process. If you don’t get shortlisted or face rejection, don’t let it discourage you. This is a common part of the process, and many more opportunities lie ahead. Stay consistent, keep improving your skills, and trust the effort you put in. If you have any questions regarding my Goldman Sachs interview experience or interview preparation in general, feel free to reach out to me at ynogale@gmail.com . I’ll try to get back as soon as possible. ALL THE BEST!
